transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Yeah, hey. So... I guess what brought me in is that I kind of went from just being a normal crew guy—you know, running the mowers, hauling brush, regular stuff—to suddenly trying to run three different bids all at once. I was calling city people, lining up all these plant suppliers... which, man, getting decent topsoil right now from the suppliers is a total nightmare because of all the rain we've had lately. The mud out at the supply yard is like knee-deep, it gets all up in the truck treads and you spend half the afternoon just hosing down the F-250 before the boss yells at you. 

But anyway, yeah, I was doing all that and just messaging literally everybody I knew about this huge park idea I had. It was like I couldn't shut it off. I was texting my buddy Dave non-stop about the layout, and he just bought this new commercial weed whacker that he won't shut up about, but I just kept going on and on about the park. So... yeah, I guess that's why I'm here.
Did you feel unusually happy or excited during the time you were working on these projects?

Yeah, I mean... I wouldn't say "happy" exactly, more like... fired up, you know? Like I felt huge, like I could take on anything, bigger than myself. But then, if one of the guys on the crew—like Steve, who's always dragging his feet anyway, I swear the guy takes a twenty-minute smoke break every time we edge a sidewalk—if he questioned my plan or told me to slow down, I'd just snap at him. Way harder than made sense, honestly. I'd just lose it. Which is weird because usually Steve and I are cool, we actually go fishing down at the reservoir sometimes. Last time we went, we caught this massive catfish, must have been like fifteen pounds, just a monster. But yeah, during that whole park bid thing, if anyone got in my way, I was just instantly pissed off.
Have you experienced any periods of feeling sad or empty in the past?

Sad or empty? I mean... I don't really think so. Not that I've noticed, anyway. I guess the only time things feel kind of empty is when winter hits and we don't get enough snow to run the plows. You know? Plowing is where the real money is at in the off-season. Last February we had that massive storm, dumped like two feet overnight, and me and the guys were out in the trucks for like thirty-six hours straight. Making absolute bank, man. We hit every commercial lot on the west side. 

But then the salt spreader on my rig jammed up because the rock salt got wet and froze solid. You gotta store that stuff under a heavy-duty tarp, but the new kid, Jason, he just left the bags out in the freezing rain. Kid is totally useless, I swear. He can't even mix the gas and oil for the two-stroke engines right. He actually burned out a perfectly good Stihl leaf blower last week because he just ran straight gas in it, didn't put any oil in the mix at all. The engine just seized up on him right in the middle of a driveway. Boss was so mad... but yeah, what were you asking? Sad? Nah, I don't really get down like that.
Have you ever felt extremely happy or on top of the world, rather than just 'fired up'?

Extremely happy? I mean, maybe not like jumping-up-and-down happy, but... I definitely felt like I was the smartest guy in the room. Like, I honestly believed I was about to become *the* guy every town around here called for sustainable landscaping. I was convinced I was going to revolutionize the whole county's park system, even though, if I'm being real, I'm still just trying to keep my small jobs paid up. 

But you know, sustainable landscaping is actually super interesting. It's all about native plants, right? Like using switchgrass and black-eyed Susans instead of just laying down Kentucky bluegrass everywhere. Bluegrass takes way too much water, especially in August when it hasn't rained in three weeks and the ground gets hard as concrete. You try pushing an aerator over that, it just bounces right off. I actually had to replace the tines on the aerator twice last summer because the soil was so compacted. The guy at the hardware store tried to sell me the cheap knock-off brand, but I told him, look man, you can't skimp on steel when you're dealing with clay soil. It just snaps. Anyway, yeah, I felt like I was going to be the king of landscaping.
How long did this 'fired up' feeling last?

How long did it last? Let's see... I guess that whole fired-up, overconfident stretch started right when I decided to remake myself for that park pitch. It went on for about two weeks, just non-stop going and going, before I finally crashed. 

Two weeks is a long time to be running that hot, honestly. Kind of like when we had to lay down sod for that new housing development out by the highway. We were on a crazy deadline because the developer wanted the houses staged for an open house that weekend. Laying sod is brutal work, man. You're just bent over all day, hauling these heavy, wet rolls of grass. And you have to get the seams perfectly tight, otherwise the edges dry out and turn brown, and then the whole lawn looks like a checkerboard. We were using this new kind of fescue blend, supposed to be drought-resistant, which is smart because the irrigation systems they install in those cookie-cutter neighborhoods are always garbage. I swear, the sprinkler heads they use are made of the cheapest plastic imaginable. One pass with a riding mower and—snap—you've got a geyser in the front yard. But yeah, about two weeks of feeling like that.
Have you had other times in your life where you felt this 'fired up' way, outside of the park bid incident?

Other times? Um... I don't know, maybe? I can't really think of another specific time right now. I mean, I'm usually pretty high energy when the spring rush hits, but I don't know if it's exactly like that park bid thing. Spring rush is just insane, though. Everybody wants their mulch laid down by Memorial Day. And people are so picky about mulch! Like, they want the double-shredded dyed black stuff, but they don't realize that the dye washes out after three heavy rainstorms and then it just looks like regular cheap woodchips anyway. I always tell them to go with natural cedar—it smells better, repels bugs, and it actually breaks down and feeds the soil. But no, they want the black dye. And then they get mad when they walk on it and track black stains onto their concrete driveways. You gotta power wash that stuff off immediately or it sets in. We use a 4000 PSI Honda pressure washer for that. Thing is a beast. You have to be careful not to get the wand too close to the concrete or it'll actually etch the surface and leave these permanent swirl marks. I saw a guy ruin a brand new patio doing that once. But yeah, I don't really remember any other times feeling like that.
Have you ever felt sad or empty for a long period of time, like more than a couple of days?

Sad or empty? Yeah. Yeah, honestly, it's... it's been hanging over me for about a year now. Just this heavy, dragging feeling. And this latest crash, after that whole park bid thing, it's the worst it's ever gotten. I just can't shake it. 

It's kind of like... you know when you're trying to clear out a massive patch of English ivy? That stuff is the absolute worst. People plant it thinking it'll look nice on a trellis, but it just takes over everything. It chokes out the trees, it ruins the masonry on houses. And you can't just pull it up, because the roots are like these thick, woody cables that go deep into the ground. You have to literally dig them out by hand, inch by inch. And even when you think you've got it all, there's always one little piece of root left behind, and next spring, boom, it's back. I spent three days last fall at this one property just ripping out ivy. My forearms were shredded, even with heavy leather gloves. You gotta wear the gauntlet style, the ones that go up past your wrists, otherwise the vines just whip you and leave these nasty scratches that always get infected because of the dirt. I tried using a brush grubber hooked up to the truck hitch once to pull a really stubborn root ball, but it just snapped the chain. So yeah, the depression is just... it's been there a year, and right now it's just really bad.
Have you had more than one episode in your life where you felt this 'fired up' way?

More than one episode? Um... I don't think so. I mean, I just said I couldn't really think of any other time I felt like that, outside of the park bid. It's hard to remember, honestly. My memory gets kind of fuzzy, especially when I'm just so drained all the time. 

It's like when you're trying to figure out what's wrong with a two-stroke engine on a weed whacker. You pull the cord and it just sputters and dies, and you can't remember if you mixed the oil and gas right. You're supposed to use a 50:1 ratio for most of the Echo trimmers we use, but the older Stihl ones take 40:1. If you run straight gas in them, even for a minute, you'll score the piston and ruin the whole block. I had a new guy do that last summer. Just grabbed the red can instead of the mixed can, fired it up, and boom, seized the engine. A brand new four-hundred-dollar piece of equipment, just garbage. You have to be so careful with the fuel lines, too. The ethanol in regular pump gas eats right through them if you let it sit over the winter. That's why you always gotta run them dry at the end of the season or use that engineered fuel in the metal cans. It costs like eight bucks a quart, but it saves you from having to rebuild the carburetor in the spring. Carburetor rebuild kits are cheap, like fifteen bucks, but taking all those tiny little diaphragms and gaskets apart is just tedious. You drop one tiny spring on the shop floor and it's gone forever. So yeah, I don't really think I've had another time feeling fired up like that.
Have you noticed any kind of regular cycle or pattern to when you feel 'fired up'?

A pattern? Um... I don't know, not really. I mean, like I said, I've only really felt that way the one time with the park bid, so there's not really a cycle to it or anything. It's just hard to track stuff like that anyway. 

It's kind of like trying to track the weather patterns for the spring planting season. You think you know when the last frost is gonna hit, right? Usually around here it's mid-April, so everyone gets all antsy and wants to put their annuals in. But you can't trust it. Two years ago we had a hard freeze on May 3rd. Wiped out an entire commercial property's worth of impatiens and begonias. Thousands of dollars just turned to mush overnight. You gotta wait until the soil temperature actually hits at least 60 degrees consistently. You can use those little meat thermometer looking things to check it, but honestly, if the oak leaves are the size of a squirrel's ear, that's the old farmer's trick to know the soil is warm enough. But even then, you get these crazy microclimates. Like, if you plant against a brick wall facing south, the brick holds the heat from the sun and it stays way warmer than a bed out in the middle of the lawn. You can actually get away with planting certain perennials a full zone outside their hardiness rating if you tuck them in right against a brick foundation. But you gotta watch out for the eaves, because if the gutters overflow, it'll just drown the roots. We do gutter cleaning too, mostly in the fall, but you'd be amazed how many people let those maple 'helicopters' clog them up in the spring. So yeah, I haven't noticed any kind of cycle or pattern to feeling fired up.
Do you think your 'fired up' episodes might happen at the same time every year?

Same time every year? No, I... I don't think so. Like I've been saying, it really was just that one time with the big park contract. So it's not like a seasonal thing or anything. 

Speaking of seasonal, though, you wouldn't believe how crazy the schedule gets right around the end of October. Everyone suddenly realizes winter is coming and they panic. "Can you do a final leaf cleanup? Can you aerate and overseed? Can you winterize the sprinkler system?" It's just non-stop calls. The sprinkler blowouts are the worst, honestly. You have to drag this massive tow-behind air compressor to every single house. It's so loud you have to wear the heavy-duty earmuffs, the ones they use at shooting ranges, or your ears will ring for three days. You hook the airline up to the backflow preventer—usually a Febco or a Watts—and just blast air through the zones until nothing but mist comes out of the heads. If you don't get all the water out, the PVC pipes will freeze and shatter underground, and then in the spring, you've got a geyser in the middle of the lawn. Digging up broken PVC in wet spring clay is a nightmare. You get covered in mud up to your elbows, and the primer and glue you use to fix the pipes smells so strong it gives you a headache. Plus, you have to wait for the glue to set before you can test the zone, so you're just standing there in the cold mud for twenty minutes. But yeah, no, I haven't noticed it happening at the same time every year or anything like that.
Do you think there was something specific that triggered you to feel 'fired up' during the park bid incident?

A trigger? Um... I don't really know. I don't think there was anything specific. I was just looking at the park plans and then I was just... going, you know? 

But looking at those plans, man, the city requires this insane amount of detail for the playground areas. You can't just use standard double-shredded hardwood mulch like you put in a front yard flower bed. You have to use engineered wood fiber. It's got all these specific safety certifications, so if a kid falls off the top of the slide, they don't crack their head open or get a massive splinter. And you can't just dump it with a wheelbarrow or a skid steer because of the retaining walls around the play area. You have to bring in a blower truck. Those trucks are massive, and they have this huge, heavy corrugated pipe you have to drag all the way across the grass. It takes like three guys just to wrangle the hose when it's full of mulch flying out at sixty miles an hour. If you lose your grip on the nozzle, it whips around like a giant snake and it will literally knock you out cold. I saw a guy get his jaw broken by one a few years ago. Plus, the dust it kicks up gets everywhere. You blow your nose at the end of the day and it's just pure black dirt. We had to use one for a middle school job once and the principal came out to complain about the noise, but it's like, how else do you expect us to move eighty cubic yards of wood chips in a single afternoon? So, yeah, I don't really know what triggered me to feel that way.
Do you think your energy levels or mood tend to change at specific times of the year?

Change at specific times of the year? My mood? Uh, no, I haven't really noticed anything like that. Like I said, it was just the one time with the park bid, so I don't really have a timeline or a season for it. 

But talking about times of the year, man, the transition from mowing season to leaf season is always a total headache. You've got half the crew still trying to finish up the final cuts on the commercial properties, and the other half are trying to get the leaf vacs mounted onto the trucks. Those leaf vacs are beasts. You have to bolt them directly onto the tailgate of the dump inserts, and if the bracket gets bent even a fraction of an inch from somebody backing into a tree over the summer, the mounting pins won't line up. You end up out there with a sledgehammer and a blowtorch just trying to force the metal back into shape so you can slide the pin through. And the impellers inside those vacs? If you suck up a hidden rock or a piece of a brick that got buried under a pile of oak leaves, it sounds like a bomb went off. It chips the impeller blades, and then the whole machine vibrates so hard it'll shake the bolts right out of the engine block. We had a guy last year suck up a stray golf ball, and it shot right through the side of the metal housing like a bullet. Almost took out a client's basement window. You have to be so careful walking the property first, but when you're rushing to beat the first snowfall, people get sloppy. So, uh, yeah, I don't think my mood changes with the seasons or anything.
Do you think your energy levels or mood might change with the seasons, even if it's not exactly the same time every year?

Change with the seasons? I mean, I don't know, I really don't think so. I haven't noticed any kind of pattern like that, even a loose one. It's just... I don't know. 

But speaking of seasons, the absolute worst part of the job has to be the early spring cleanups. Everyone wants their yard looking perfect the second the snow melts, but the ground is just pure mush. You can't even get a zero-turn mower on the turf without leaving ruts six inches deep. We have to do everything by hand. You're out there with a metal spring rake, just dragging it through this heavy, wet, matted down grass, trying to pull up all the dead thatch and whatever garbage blew into the yard over the winter. It destroys your shoulders. And the dog poop, man. People just let their dogs go in the yard all winter and never pick it up because it's buried in the snow. Then the snow melts, and you've got this minefield of soggy, half-frozen mess everywhere. If you hit one with a string trimmer, it just vaporizes and coats your shins. You have to wear those rubber muck boots, but even then, the smell just bakes into the plastic. We had a new guy quit by noon on his first day last April because he slipped on a slope and basically body-surfed through a whole patch of it. I told him he should have worn cleats, but he didn't listen. So, yeah, no, I don't think my energy levels really shift with the seasons or anything.
Do you feel like your mood or energy changes at all during different times of the year?

Doc, I feel like you keep asking me about the calendar. Like I said, no, I don't really notice my mood changing with the time of year. My energy is just my energy, you know? 

But honestly, the only thing that really changes during different times of the year is the equipment maintenance. Like, right before winter, you have to winterize all the two-stroke engines. The weed whackers, the hedge trimmers, the chainsaws. If you leave regular pump gas sitting in those tiny carburetors over the winter, the ethanol completely eats away the fuel lines. They turn to absolute mush. Come spring, you go to pull the starter cord and it just dumps gas everywhere. You either have to drain every single tank and run them completely dry, or you have to pay out the nose for that pre-mixed engineered fuel in the metal cans. It's like eight bucks a quart, which is a total ripoff, but it saves you from having to rebuild twenty carburetors in March. My boss tried to cheap out two years ago and just dumped some cheap fuel stabilizer in the big gas caddies, but he didn't mix it right. We spent the first three weeks of April just taking apart carburetors on the tailgate of the trucks, spraying carb cleaner everywhere. That stuff burns so bad if you get it in a cut on your hands. And you always have cuts on your hands from pruning the barberry bushes. Have you ever dealt with barberry? It's got these tiny little thorns that break off under your skin and just fester for days. You have to dig them out with a sewing needle. Anyway, yeah, I don't know why we keep coming back to the seasons. I just don't feel any different.
Do you feel more energized or experience mood changes during certain seasons of the year?

Okay, is this a trick question? Because I swear you've asked me this exact same thing like four times now. No, Doc. No seasons. Winter, spring, summer, fall—my brain doesn't care what month it is on the calendar. I don't get energized just because it's July or whatever. 

I mean, honestly, the only time I get a massive spike in energy during a specific season is late August when I hit a yellow jacket nest. Have you ever hit a ground nest with a weed whacker? It is pure chaos. You're just walking along, edging a garden bed, minding your own business, and suddenly it's like the ground literally boils. They don't just sting you once and die like a honeybee, they latch onto your clothes and just keep jabbing you. We had a guy—not the dog poop guy from before, a different guy—who hit a bald-faced hornet nest the size of a basketball that was completely hidden inside a giant rhododendron. He dropped a brand new Stihl trimmer, just left it running right there in the bush, and sprinted halfway down the street screaming. We had to wait until the engine ran out of gas, and then go back at night with two cans of that foaming wasp spray that shoots twenty feet just to get the equipment back. And the worst part is, the clients come out and get mad that you didn't finish the trimming. Like, lady, I'm not going to the hospital for your hydrangeas. You can wait until tomorrow. 

But yeah, unless I'm literally sprinting for my life from a swarm of hornets, my energy doesn't change with the seasons at all. I really don't know how else to tell you that.
Do you think your periods of feeling fired up could be part of a larger pattern of mood swings?

A larger pattern? I don't know about a pattern, but... yeah, before I completely crashed, I did feel really fired up. Like, I had this energy where I just felt almost... bigger than myself, you know? Like I could handle anything, completely invincible. But the problem was, if anyone got in my way, I'd just lose it. Like if a coworker questioned my plan for a job or told me to slow down, I'd snap at him way, way harder than made sense. 

Which reminds me of this one time we were putting in a massive hardscape patio. I had the whole layout mapped out in my head, exactly how the pavers were going to interlock. And the foreman—this guy, Gary, who thinks he knows everything just because he's been doing it for twenty years—he comes over and tells me my base isn't level. I mean, I had already compacted the crushed stone, screeded the sand, it was perfect. But he puts his four-foot level on it and starts tapping it with his boot, acting like I don't know what I'm doing. I just saw red. I threw my rubber mallet across the yard—it actually bounced off the client's vinyl fence, thank God it didn't crack it—and I just started screaming at him. I told him if he wanted to lay the pavers himself he could do it on his hands and knees all weekend. He just stared at me. 

But honestly, the worst part about laying pavers isn't even the leveling. It's the polymeric sand at the end. You sweep it into the joints, and you have to make sure there's absolutely no dust left on top of the stones before you wet it down. Because if you wet it while there's still sand dust on the surface, it activates the polymers and basically glues a hazy white film over the entire patio. You can't get it off. You have to use this harsh efflorescence cleaner that smells like straight acid and burns your lungs. We had a guy do that once on a dark charcoal paver job, and it ruined the whole thing. We had to power wash it for three days straight. But anyway, yeah, I definitely felt fired up and irritable before I crashed, but I don't know if it's a pattern.
Do you think your periods of feeling fired up and then crashing into a low mood might be related to each other?

Related? I mean, I guess? I don't really know. It’s like, you go way up, and then eventually you just run out of gas and crash. But I don't know if one actually causes the other, you know? It's just... they both happen. 

Crashing is awful, though. Honestly, talking about crashing, the worst crash I ever saw at work was on a zero-turn mower. Have you ever driven a zero-turn on wet morning grass? They are completely useless on a hill. The tires just lose all traction, and because you steer with the rear wheels, once you start sliding, you are literally just a passenger. You can pull the lap bars all the way back into reverse, but you just keep gliding down the slope like you're on ice. This new kid we hired slid a sixty-inch Scag mower right into a muddy drainage ditch. The wheels just dug in and spun, making these massive, deep ruts. We had to hook up a heavy-duty tow strap to the F-250 just to rip it out of there, and then we had to spend three hours fixing the turf. You have to fill the ruts with a mix of topsoil and sand, tamp it all down, seed it, and then cover it with straw so the birds don't eat the seed. And the whole time, the client is just standing on his back deck drinking coffee, watching us ruin his perfect lawn. It's an absolute nightmare. 

But yeah, as for my moods... I really couldn't tell you if they're connected like a chain reaction or something. I just know I feel invincible for a bit, and then later on, I'm just completely dead to the world.
Do you think your periods of feeling extremely fired up and then crashing into a low mood might be two sides of the same emotional state?

Two sides of the same state? Uh, I don't know. Maybe? I guess it's like a battery or something. You're fully charged and then you're dead. But I don't really sit around analyzing if they're, like, the same thing. I'm just trying to get through the day. 

Speaking of batteries, you would not believe how many guys forget to charge the batteries for the electric blowers. We've been trying to switch over to battery-powered equipment for some of the smaller residential properties because the noise ordinances in these rich neighborhoods are getting ridiculous. You can't even start a gas backpack blower before 8:00 AM without someone calling the town code enforcement. So we got these massive lithium-ion backpack blowers. They weigh a ton, honestly, heavier than the gas ones. But the problem is, if the crew from the day before doesn't plug the batteries into the charging bank in the shop overnight, you get out to the first job at 7:30 AM, hit the trigger, and it just flashes a red light and dies. Then you're stuck using a hand broom on a massive driveway like it's 1950. 

I actually had to use a push broom on this massive aggregate concrete driveway once because of that. Do you know how hard it is to sweep wet pine needles off exposed aggregate? It's like trying to sweep Velcro. You just end up smearing them around. 

But, uh, what were you asking? Two sides of the same thing? Yeah, I have no idea. I just know I go way up and then way down. That's about it.
Do you think your periods of feeling extremely fired up and then crashing into a low mood might be symptoms of a larger mental health condition?

A larger mental health condition? I mean, I never really thought about it like a sickness or a condition or whatever. It's just my life. I just thought I was wired differently, you know? Like some people just run hotter than others. 

You know who runs hot? The guys who have to do the asphalt patching in August. We don't do full paving, but we do hot patch repairs for some commercial lots we maintain. And let me tell you, when the ambient temperature is ninety-five degrees with eighty percent humidity, and you're standing over a pile of asphalt that's literally three hundred degrees, it messes with your head. You can feel the heat radiating right through the soles of your work boots. If you don't wear thick enough socks, your feet actually start to blister just from standing on it. And the smell—it's this thick, oily, tar smell that just coats the back of your throat and you can't taste anything else for two days. We had a guy pass out once, just completely locked his knees and went over backward onto the grass median. We had to drag him into the shade and pour ice water from the Igloo cooler all over his chest. You really gotta hydrate before you even get to the site, or you're already behind. 

But yeah, a mental health condition? I don't know about all that. I'm just here because the crashes are getting so bad I can't even get out of bed to go to work, and the boss is threatening to let me go. I'm not trying to put a label on it, I just need it to stop.
Do you think your periods of feeling extremely fired up and then crashing into a low mood might be symptoms of something bigger, like bipolar disorder?

Bipolar disorder? Man, I don't know. That sounds... intense. Like, isn't that when people go totally crazy and end up in the hospital? I've never been hospitalized or anything. I just get really pumped up and then I crash hard. I guess maybe it could be? But honestly, I try not to read into that medical stuff too much. 

It reminds me of when my buddy Dave started looking up his symptoms on WebMD because his elbow was hurting. He was convinced he had bone cancer or some rare degenerative disease. Turns out it was just tennis elbow from running the string trimmer too much. You know those big straight-shaft Echo trimmers? They vibrate like crazy. If you don't wear the anti-vibration gloves, it sends shockwaves right up your forearm into your elbow joint. And Dave, he’s this huge guy, but he refuses to use the shoulder strap. He just carries the whole weight of the machine on his right arm for eight hours a day, just edging miles of sidewalks. I kept telling him, "Dave, just clip the harness on, it distributes the weight," but he’s stubborn as a mule. He finally had to go to physical therapy for six weeks, doing all these weird stretches with rubber bands just to be able to hold a coffee cup again. The physical therapist told him if he kept doing it without the strap, he’d permanently wreck his tendons. 

So yeah, looking up diseases and labels... it usually just freaks you out for no reason. But I mean, if you think it's bipolar or whatever, you're the doctor. I just know I can't keep living like this where I can't even drag myself out of bed half the time.

doctor.intent: determine presence of elevated mood
doctor.question: Did you feel unusually happy or excited during the time you were working on these projects?

But even then, you get these crazy microclimates. Like, if you plant against a brick wall facing south, the brick holds the heat from the sun and it stays way warmer than a bed out in the middle of the lawn. You can actually get away with planting certain perennials a full zone outside their hardiness rating if you tuck them in right against a brick foundation. Speaking of seasonal, though, you wouldn't believe how crazy the schedule gets right around the end of October. Everyone suddenly realizes winter is coming and they panic. "Can you do a final leaf cleanup? Can you aerate and overseed? Can you winterize the sprinkler system?" It's just non-stop calls. The sprinkler blowouts are the worst, honestly. You hook the airline up to the backflow preventer—usually a Febco or a Watts—and just blast air through the zones until nothing but mist comes out of the heads. If you don't get all the water out, the PVC pipes will freeze and shatter underground, and then in the spring, you've got a geyser in the middle of the lawn. Digging up broken PVC in wet spring clay is a nightmare. You get covered in mud up to your elbows, and the primer and glue you use to fix the pipes smells so strong it gives you a headache. Plus, you have to wait for the glue to set before you can test the zone, so you're just standing there in the cold mud for twenty minutes. We had a guy pass out once, just completely locked his knees and went over backward onto the grass median. We had to drag him into the shade and pour ice water from the Igloo cooler all over his chest. You really gotta hydrate before you even get to the site, or you're already behind. 

But yeah, a mental health condition? I don't know about all that. I'm just here because the crashes are getting so bad I can't even get out of bed to go to work, and the boss is threatening to let me go. I'm not trying to put a label on it, I just need it to stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's mood swings are a result of a bipolar disorder
doctor.question: Do you think your periods of feeling extremely fired up and then crashing into a low mood might be symptoms of something bigger, like bipolar disorder?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my insight into my condition and whether I think I might have bipolar disorder, which is not covered by any specific symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Bipolar disorder? Man, I don't know. That sounds... intense. Like, isn't that when people go totally crazy and end up in the hospital? I've never been hospitalized or anything. I just get really pumped up and then I crash hard. I guess maybe it could be? But honestly, I try not to read into that medical stuff too much. 

It reminds me of when my buddy Dave started looking up his symptoms on WebMD because his elbow was hurting. He was convinced he had bone cancer or some rare degenerative disease. Turns out it was just tennis elbow from running the string trimmer too much. You know those big straight-shaft Echo trimmers? They vibrate like crazy. If you don't wear the anti-vibration gloves, it sends shockwaves right up your forearm into your elbow joint. And Dave, he’s this huge guy, but he refuses to use the shoulder strap. He just carries the whole weight of the machine on his right arm for eight hours a day, just edging miles of sidewalks. I kept telling him, "Dave, just clip the harness on, it distributes the weight," but he’s stubborn as a mule. He finally had to go to physical therapy for six weeks, doing all these weird stretches with rubber bands just to be able to hold a coffee cup again. The physical therapist told him if he kept doing it without the strap, he’d permanently wreck his tendons. 

So yeah, looking up diseases and labels... it usually just freaks you out for no reason. But I mean, if you think it's bipolar or whatever, you're the doctor. I just know I can't keep living like this where I can't even drag myself out of bed half the time.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits symptoms of manic episodes, including increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and irritability, followed by depressive episodes, which are characteristic of Bipolar I Disorder.
